extracted.intended_audience: editors, journalists, cartoonists and publishers (Australian news media) and those interested in media standards/adjudications
extracted.subtask_description: Adjudication applying the Australian Press Council's Standards of Practice (General Principle 6) to an editorial cartoon, assessing whether the publication took reasonable steps to avoid causing or contributing materially to substantial offence, distress or prejudice. Focus is on editorial/cartoon content, depiction of ethnic groups, and public interest defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Principle 6 — reasonable steps to avoid causing offence or prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: "Publications must take reasonable steps to: Avoid causing or contributing materially to substantial offence, distress or prejudice, or a substantial risk to health or safety, unless doing so is sufficiently in the public interest."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the Council's core standard applied in the adjudication. It requires publications to proactively take reasonable steps to prevent materially contributing to substantial offence, distress or prejudice (or substantial risk to health/safety), unless a sufficiently strong public interest justifies the harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartoons receive significant latitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The Council recognises that cartoons are expressions of opinion that often use exaggeration and absurdity to make a point on serious issues. For this reason, the Council has given significant latitude to cartoons when considering whether a publication has taken reasonable steps to avoid substantial offence, distress or prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial cartoons are afforded greater leeway because of their satirical/exaggerated form. However, this latitude is not absolute and must be balanced against other standards (e.g., avoiding substantial offence/prejudice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest balancing — freedom of expression versus preventing offence/prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: The Council recognises the significant public interest in allowing freedom of expression must be weighed against the equally significant public interest in not causing or contributing to offence or prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating potentially offensive material, the Council balances the public interest in open debate and expression with the public interest in preventing harm. A public interest justification must be strong enough to outweigh the harm caused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial intention is relevant but not determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: The Council accepts that the intention of the cartoon was to comment on the political debate surrounding the immigration numbers and not on who or where the immigrants were arriving from. The Council also accepts that it was not the cartoonist's intention to cause offence or prejudice. However, the Council considers that the depiction... is offensive and prejudicial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A publisher's stated intent (e.g., to comment on numbers rather than ethnicity) will be taken into account, but a lack of intent to offend does not absolve the publisher if the depiction nonetheless materially causes substantial offence or prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depicting ethnic groups inaccurately or using stereotypical features can be offensive and prejudicial
rubrics_metrics.description: The depiction of the immigrants, which it notes is not reflective of the ethnic and geographical composition of migrant arrivals into Australia, together with the raising of the drawbridge, implies that such immigrants are undesirable. The depiction of such people as mostly brown skinned, with prominent facial features and attire that reflects a stereotypical portrayal of people from the Middle East and Africa, including Muslims, is offensive and prejudicial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrayals that rely on stereotypical physical characteristics, attire or presumed ethnicity — particularly when not reflective of the factual composition of the group depicted — can materially contribute to prejudice and offence and thus breach the standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual considerations (e.g., political debate, metaphor) are important but insufficient alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The publication said the cartoon should be considered in context of the political debate concerning Australia’s dramatic 73% increase in immigration and whether Australia could sustain such levels. The publication said the cartoon seeks to illustrate the increase in immigration by drawing a crowd of entrants coming in Australia's front door, which is depicted metaphorically as a drawbridge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context such as topical political debate or use of metaphor may explain why a publisher produced a particular depiction and is considered in assessment. However, context does not automatically justify representations that materially cause substantial offence or prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest defence must be sufficient to justify substantial offence/prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: While the Council recognises the public interest in commenting on the political debate around immigration, the Council does not consider it was sufficient to justify the substantial offence and prejudice caused or contributed to in choosing to depict the immigrants in the manner in which it did.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A public interest claim (e.g., contributing to debate on immigration numbers) will not excuse a publication if the Council determines the public interest is insufficient to justify the level of offence or prejudice resulting from the depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to take reasonable steps can constitute a breach
rubrics_metrics.description: Accordingly, the Council concludes that the publication failed to take reasonable steps to avoid causing or contributing materially to substantial offence and prejudice in breach of General Principle 6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Council finds a publication did not take reasonable preventative steps in composing or publishing material that foreseeably causes substantial offence or prejudice, the publication will be found in breach of the standard.
